# Use Case

## Background

It is hard to talk about the history of the **Philadelphia Chinatown** without the construction of **I-676**, also known as the **Vine Street Expressway**. Although the highway serves as a significant thoroughfare through Center City Philadelphia, the indispensable repercussion on the adjacent neighborhoods still lingers today. Consequences of the highway such as demolishment of buildings, pedestrian safety threats, traffic congestion, as well as noise and air pollutions had been harming Chinatown and its surrounding neighborhoods over the past decades and are yet to be addressed.

Standing in opposition to the issues, [City of Philadelphia Office of Transportation and Infrastructure and Sustainability (OTIS)](https://www.phila.gov/departments/office-of-transportation-and-infrastructure-systems/) brought forth the plan of capping sections of the expressway as a solution to address its historical harms on the Chinatown region. This “cap”, named **the Chinatown Stitch project**, aimed to create a safe and equitable green space for the public that would reconnect areas north and south to the Vine Street expressway. Receiving funds from the US department of Transportation and the local organizations, the construction of the Chinatown Stitch will start in 2027 and is expected to be completed in early 2030.

This purpose of this study is to help OTIS **understand the housing market of Philadelphia Chinatown region before and after the implementation of the Chinatown Stitch**. The first part of the study will focus the effects of highways on sales prices in the study region as well as the entire Philadelphia. House prices will then be estimated using **three predictive models under three different future scenarios**: business as usual without the implementation of the Chinatown Stitch, business as usual with the implementation of the Chinatown Stitch, and an alternative future in which the Chinatown Stitch significantly reshapes the urban landscape of the study region.

![](Final%20R%20Markdown/Images/background.png)

Three study areas are used in the analysis to reveal the effects of I-676 on the land market of the Chinatown region.

-   **Referable study area (Philadelphia):** to analyse the impact of different highways on the surrounding land markets in the context of the city.
-   **Main study area (10 block groups):** to figure out the correlation between I-676 and property sales price and make future predictions based on three potential scenarios.
-   **Compared study area ([north]{style="color: #eb5600;"} and [south]{style="color: #1a9988;"} sides):** to investigate the different situations of the Chinatown region under the construction of I-676.

In the vision of **a city park** in the future, the Chinatown Stitch will bring vitality to local residents and visitors along with other green spaces. Connected with the Stitch, the **Rail Park** in the [north (Callowhill neighborhood)]{style="color: #eb5600;"} is still in construction and will make an impact years later. With a foundation of **cultural and commercial resources**, the [southern part (Chinatown neighborhood)]{style="color: #1a9988;"} will provide services to the surrounding area, including the city center of Philadelphia.

# Data Wrangling

## Property Data

Our primary variable of interest, **property price**, is sourced from the [Philadelphia Properties and Assessment History](https://opendataphilly.org/datasets/philadelphia-properties-and-assessment-history/) dataset available on Open Data Philly. This dataset includes variables such as `sale_price`, number of bedrooms, parcel number, and property condition. To prepare the data for analysis, we apply the following preprocessing steps related to sale date, inflation adjustment, geographic transformation, and handling of missing values:

+ **Sale Date (Philadelphia Focus)**: To ensure price comparability, we limit our analysis to properties sold **between 2020 and 2024** within Philadelphia.

+ **Inflation Adjustment**: Sale prices are adjusted for inflation using the **Consumer Price Index (CPI)**, normalized to December 2024 values.

+ **Price Range Filtering**: We begin by removing records with **implausibly low sale prices (below $100)**. Then, to reduce the influence of outliers and enhance generalizability, we **trim both the bottom and top 5%** of the price distribution.

+ **Geographic Transformation**: Since spatial proximity to highways and other features influences property values, we reproject coordinates to **NAD83 / Pennsylvania South (EPSG: 2272)** for accurate spatial analysis.

+ **Missing Data Imputation**: Missing values for **zoning**, **central air**, and **year built** are filled using current property characteristics where available.



```{r property_data_adj, eval=FALSE}
#### clean data for city wise - sale price
cpi_data <- st_read("E:/Spring/Practicum/DataAnalysis/Chinatown/Dataset/property/cpi_data.csv")
colnames(cpi_data) <- c("half1", "half2", "cpi_date")
cpi_long <- cpi_data %>%
  mutate(
    Jan = `half1`, Feb = `half1`, Mar = `half1`, Apr = `half1`, May = `half1`, Jun = `half1`,
    Jul = `half2`, Aug = `half2`, Sep = `half2`, Oct = `half2`, Nov = `half2`, Dec = `half2`
  ) %>%
  select(-half1, -half2) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -cpi_date, names_to = "Month", values_to = "CPI") %>%
  mutate(
    Month = match(Month, month.abb),
    date = as.Date(paste(cpi_date, Month, "01", sep = "-"))  
  ) %>%
  select(date, CPI)

property_philly <- property %>%
  mutate(sale_date = as.Date(sale_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d")) %>%
  filter(sale_date >= as.Date("2020-01-01") & sale_date <= as.Date("2024-12-31"))%>%
  filter(!is.na(sale_price), !is.na(total_livable_area))%>%
  mutate(
    sale_month = floor_date(sale_date, "month"))%>%
  left_join(cpi_long, by = c("sale_month" = "date"))%>%
  mutate(CPI = as.numeric(CPI))%>%
  mutate(adj_sale_price = sale_price * (340.331/CPI))%>%
  select(-sale_month, -recording_date,  -other_building, 
         -assessment_date, -mailing_address_2, mailing_city_state, mailing_care_of)

property_philly_100 <- property_philly %>%
  filter(adj_sale_price >= 100)

q_philly <- quantile(property_philly_100$adj_sale_price, probs = c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE)

property_philly_filtered <- property_philly %>%
  filter(adj_sale_price >= q_philly[1], adj_sale_price <= q_philly[2]) %>%
  st_transform('EPSG:2272')
###################################################################################################
# Study Area
property_studyarea <-property_original %>%
  mutate(sale_date = as.Date(sale_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(sale_price))%>%
  filter(sale_date <= as.Date("2024-12-31"))%>%
  mutate(
    sale_date = as.Date(sale_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d"), 
    sale_month = floor_date(sale_date, "month"))%>%
  left_join(cpi_long, by = c("sale_month" = "date"))%>%
  mutate(CPI = as.numeric(CPI))%>%
  mutate(adj_sale_price = sale_price * (340.331/CPI)) %>%
  select(-sale_month,-recording_date,  -other_building, 
         -assessment_date, -mailing_address_2, mailing_city_state, mailing_care_of, -state_code)%>%
  relocate(adj_sale_price, sale_price, .after = 2)

property_stuyarea_100 <- property_studyarea %>%
  filter(adj_sale_price >= 100)

q_studyarea <- quantile(property_stuyarea_100$adj_sale_price, probs = c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE)

property_studyarea_filtered <- property_studyarea %>%
  filter(adj_sale_price >= q_studyarea[1], adj_sale_price <= q_studyarea[2])

# join attributes - I676(NS) - nhood1 (neighborhoods in study area)
property_studyarea_filtered_changed <- rbind(
    property_studyarea_filtered %>% st_intersection(studyarea_north["geometry"]) %>%
      mutate(I676_NS = "north"),
    property_studyarea_filtered %>% st_intersection(studyarea_south["geometry"]) %>%
      mutate(I676_NS = "south")
  )

#Features clean up for future FE and modeling
## Zoning
property_studyarea_filtered_changed <- property_studyarea_filtered_changed %>%
  select(1:2, zoning, location, everything())

property_studyarea_filtered_changed <- property_studyarea_filtered_changed %>%
  mutate(zoning = case_when(
    location == "1310-16 VINE ST" ~ "CMX4",   
    location == "252-56 N 13TH ST" ~ "CMX4",
    location == "255-57 N BROAD ST" ~ "CMX4",
    location == "451 N 12TH ST" ~ "CMX3",
    location == "453 N 12TH ST" ~"CMX3",
    location == "447 N 12TH ST" ~ "CMX3",
    location == "1108 BUTTONWOOD ST" ~ "CMX3",
    location == "1104 BUTTONWOOD ST" ~ "CMX3",
    location == "256-60 N MARVINE ST" ~ "CMX4",
    location == "820 VINE ST" ~ "CMX4",
    TRUE ~ zoning                        
  ))

## central air
target_locations_N <- c(
                      "1232 SUMMER ST", 
                      "1030 BRANDYWINE ST",
                      "214 N 12TH ST",
                      "1021 SPRING ST")

property_studyarea_filtered_changed <- property_studyarea_filtered_changed %>%
  mutate(
    central_air = ifelse(location %in% target_locations_N & central_air == "N", "Y", central_air)
  )
## year built - clean up values of 1 and delete the other rows which are parking plot properties that have no year_built data
valid_locations <- c(
  "305-09 N 12TH ST",
  "1008-16 WOOD ST",
  "1004-06 WOOD ST",
  "211 N CAMAC ST",
  "231-33 N BROAD ST",
  "225-27 N 12TH ST"
)
property_studyarea_filtered_changed <- property_studyarea_filtered_changed %>%
  filter(location != "711-39 SPRING GARDEN ST") %>%
  mutate(year_built = as.numeric(year_built)) %>%
  mutate(
    year_built = case_when(
      location == "305-09 N 12TH ST" & year_built < 1750 ~ 1950,
      location == "1008-16 WOOD ST" & year_built < 1750 ~ 1978,
      location == "1004-06 WOOD ST" & year_built < 1750 ~ 1920,
      location == "211 N CAMAC ST" & year_built < 1750 ~ 1900,
      location == "231-33 N BROAD ST" & year_built < 1750 ~ 2020,
      location == "225-27 N 12TH ST" & year_built < 1750 ~ 2024,
      
      !is.na(year_built) & year_built < 1750 &
        !(location %in% c(
          "305-09 N 12TH ST",
          "1008-16 WOOD ST",
          "1004-06 WOOD ST",
          "211 N CAMAC ST",
          "231-33 N BROAD ST",
          "225-27 N 12TH ST"
        )) ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ year_built
    )
  )
```

```{r neighborhood_process}
calculate_nearest_distance <- function(set_points, other_layer) {
  nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(set_points, other_layer)
  st_distance(set_points, other_layer[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE) %>% as.numeric()
}

Luming_property <- property_original %>%
  dplyr::select(objectid, geometry, sale_price) %>%
  rename(orig_objectid = objectid)

Luming_property <- Luming_property %>%
  mutate(distance_to_city_hall = st_distance(., city_hall) %>% as.numeric()) %>%
  mutate(
    distance_to_nearest_transit = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, transit),
    distance_to_nearest_hospital = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, hospital),
    distance_to_nearest_school = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, school),
    distance_to_nearest_park = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, park),
    distance_to_nearest_water = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, water),
    distance_to_nearest_bikelane = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, bike_network),
    distance_to_I676 = calculate_nearest_distance(geometry, I_676)
  ) %>%
  st_join(nhoods["NAME"], left = TRUE) %>%
  rename(nhoods_name = NAME) %>%
  st_join(landuse_rename["landuse"], left = TRUE) %>%
  st_join(retail[, c("LPSS_PER1000", "HPSS_PER1000")], left = TRUE)

Luming_property <- Luming_property %>% 
    mutate(
      crime_nn1 = nn_function(st_coordinates(Luming_property),
                              st_coordinates(phillyCrimes), k = 1),

      crime_nn2 = nn_function(st_coordinates(Luming_property),
                              st_coordinates(phillyCrimes), k = 2),

      crime_nn3 = nn_function(st_coordinates(Luming_property),
                              st_coordinates(phillyCrimes), k = 3),

      crime_nn4 = nn_function(st_coordinates(Luming_property),
                              st_coordinates(phillyCrimes), k = 4),
      
      crime_nn5 = nn_function(st_coordinates(Luming_property), 
                              st_coordinates(phillyCrimes), k = 5))
```

## Philadelphia Scale Analysis

Before jumping into modeling, we first explored the relationship between **distance to highway** and **property prices**. We used property data from OPA Philadelphia that was cleaned to include only the data from the last five years (Jan. 1st, 2020 to Dec. 31st, 2024) with prices adjusted for inflation after removing extreme outliers and improbable values (keeping rows with property price within the 5th and 95th percentile), and keeping properties with total area of over 100 square feet (see map below for the properties included in this analysis).

Our **Philadelphia Scale Analysis** looks at properties (of all kinds, not limited to housing properties) within 500 m of Philadelphia's main highways -- [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"} on the East, [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"} on the West, [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"} in the North, and [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} through the city. We saw the following trends in property prices.

```{r prep_500m_highway_data, quiet = TRUE, results = 'hide'}
# create 500m buffer around philly highways
buff500 <- 500 * 3.28084
hiway_500buff <- st_union(st_buffer(philly_highways, buff500))

# read in pre-saved file
prop500 <- st_read("Dataset/phl_properties_dist2highway/philly_prop500_dst2hghwy_250421.geojson") %>%
  mutate(closest_highway = factor(closest_highway, levels = c("US-1", "I-76", "I-676", "I-95")))
```

```{r map_prop500}
# map of properties within 500m of highway cored by which highway they're closest to
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = philly_bounds, fill = "#c9b887", color = "grey") +
  geom_sf(data = hydro, fill = "#7d97c7", color = "transparent") +
  geom_sf(data = philly_parks, fill = "#6b9169", color = "transparent") +
  geom_sf(data = hiway_500buff,
          color = "transparent", fill = "grey", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = prop500,
          aes(color = closest_highway), size = 0.3,
          show.legend = F) +
  geom_sf(data = philly_highways,
          color = "black") +
  
  # add custom colors
  scale_color_manual(values = c("US-1" = "#1a9988",
                                "I-76" = "#eb5600",
                                "I-95" = "#eba075",
                                "I-676" = "#7fe3d6")) +
  # labels for highway names
  geom_text(aes(label = "US-1",
                x = 2700000,
                y = 256453.2),
            color = "#1a9988") +
  geom_text(aes(label = "I-76",
                x = 2680000,

  geom_text(aes(label = "I-95",
                x = 2705200,

  geom_text(aes(label = "I-676",
                x = 2694000,
                y = 243000),
            color = "#7fe3d6") +
```

```{r prop500_med_saleprices}
# median sale prices to talk about in the text
med_price_us1 <- round(median(prop500 %>% 
                          filter(closest_highway == "US-1") %>% 
                          pull(adj_sale_price)))

med_price_i76 <- round(median(prop500 %>% 
                          filter(closest_highway == "I-76") %>% 
                          pull(adj_sale_price)))

med_price_i95 <- round(median(prop500 %>% 
                          filter(closest_highway == "I-95") %>% 
                          pull(adj_sale_price)))

med_price_676 <- round(median(prop500 %>% 
                          filter(closest_highway == "I-676") %>% 
                          pull(adj_sale_price)))

# count of properties included in analysis 
prop_count <- prop500 %>% 
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  group_by(closest_highway) %>% 
  summarise(count = n())

prop_count_676 <- prop_count %>% 
  filter(grepl("676", closest_highway)) %>% 
  pull(count)

prop_count_us1 <- prop_count %>% 
  filter(grepl("US", closest_highway)) %>% 
  pull(count)

prop_count_i76 <- prop_count %>% 
  filter(grepl("-76", closest_highway)) %>% 
  pull(count)

prop_count_i95 <- prop_count %>% 
  filter(grepl("95", closest_highway)) %>% 
  pull(count)
```

`r paste0(substr(nrow(prop500), 1, 2), ",", substr(nrow(prop500), 3, 5))` total properties were included in this analysis. We see that the distribution of log sale prices of properties within 500m of highways in Philadelphia generally follow a normal distribution.

Though there aren't as many properties near [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} (`r prop_count_676` properties) as there are near the other highways, they are most expensive group with a median property price of **`r paste0('$', substr(med_price_676, 1, 3), ',', substr(med_price_676, 4, 9))`**. 

Properties near [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"} and [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"} are among a similar range of prices with median property prices being **`r paste0('$', substr(med_price_i95, 1, 3), ',', substr(med_price_i95, 4, 9))`** and **`r paste0('$', substr(med_price_i76, 1, 3), ',', substr(med_price_i76, 4, 9))`**, respectively, though there are almost five times as many properties near [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"} compared to [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"} (`r paste0(substr(prop_count_i95,1,1), ",", substr(prop_count_i95, 2,4))` and `r paste0(substr(prop_count_i76,1,1), ",", substr(prop_count_i76, 2,4))` properties around [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"} and [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, respectively). 

Finally, there are many properties within 500m of [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"} (`r paste0(substr(prop_count_us1,1,1), ",", substr(prop_count_us1, 2,4))` properties), but the median property price was lowest compared to other highways at **`r paste0('$', substr(med_price_us1, 1, 3), ',', substr(med_price_us1, 4, 9))`**.

```{r prop500_scatter}
# models + beta coefficients
coef_us1 <- round(
  summary(
    lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway,
       data = prop500 %>% 
         filter(grepl("US", closest_highway)))
    )$coefficients[2,1], 3) # *** p < 0.001

coef_i76 <- round(
  summary(
    lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway, 
       data = prop500 %>% 
         filter(grepl("-76", closest_highway)))
    )$coefficients[2,1], 3) # ** p < 0.05

coef_i95 <- round(
  summary(
    lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway, 
       data = prop500 %>% 
         filter(grepl("95", closest_highway)))
    )$coefficients[2,1], 3) # *** p < 0.001

coef_i676 <- round(
  summary(
    lm(log_price ~ log_dist_to_closest_highway, 
       data = prop500 %>%
         filter(grepl("676", closest_highway)))
    )$coefficients[2,1], 3) # not statistically significant, p = 0.0693

scatter_4highways <- 
  ggplot(data = prop500, 
       aes(x = log_dist_to_closest_highway, y = log_price, 
           color = closest_highway, fill = closest_highway)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .2, size = 0.3, show.legend = F) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", size = 1.2, show.legend = F) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("US-1" = "#1a9988",
                                "I-76" = "#eb5600",
                                "I-95" = "#eba075",
                                "I-676" = "#7fe3d6")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("US-1" = "#1a9988",
                               "I-76" = "#eb5600",
                               "I-95" = "#eba075",
                               "I-676" = "#7fe3d6")) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("US-1:", coef_us1),
                x = 4.25,
                y = 11.75),
            color = "#1a9988", 
            show.legend = F) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("I-76:", coef_i76),
                x = 4.25,
                y = 12.75),
            color = "#eb5600",
            show.legend = F) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("I-95:", coef_i95),
                x = 4.25,
                y = 13.25),
            color = "#eba075",
            show.legend = F) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("I-676:", coef_i676),
                x = 4.25,
                y = 13.75),
            color = "#7fe3d6",
            show.legend = F) +
  labs(title = "Property Price (log) as a function of Distance to Closest Highway (log)",
       subtitle = "Properties within 500m of highways",
       x = "Log Distance to Closest Highway",
       y = "Log Property Sale Price") +
  theme_minimal()

scatter_4highways

```

The scatter plot above shows the relationship between distance to highway and property price along with the regression coefficients for each highway. We observe that without controlling for anything else, property prices generally increase (albeit by very little) as we move away from a highway which tracks with our literature review of highway effects on property prices. 

When predicting property price, the beta coefficient for log distance to highway is `r coef_i676`, `r coef_i76`, and `r coef_us1` for [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, and [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, respectively (note that the though the beta coefficients were significant with p < 0.01 for [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"} and [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, it was not statistically significant for [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} with a p = 0.069). 

For every 1% increase in distance from [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_i676 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, this means that if a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway, we can expect a similar property a block further from the highway to be about **`r paste0("$", round((4^coef_i676)*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** (assuming a block is about 200m). For every 1% increase in distance from [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_i76 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`, meaning a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway would be about **`r paste0("$", round((4^coef_i76)*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** if it were a block further from the highway. For every 1% increase in distance from [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_us1 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`, meaning a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway would be about **`r paste0("$", round((4^coef_us1)*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** if it were a block further from the highway.

The exception here is for properties within 500m of [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"}, where the beta coefficient for log distance to highway is `r coef_i95` (p < 0.001). For every 1% increase in distance from [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"}, property price decreases by `r paste0(round(abs(1.01^coef_i95 - 1), 4)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, this means that if a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway, we can expect a similar property a block further from the highway to be about **`r paste0("$", 100000 - round((4^coef_i95), 5)*100000)` less expensive**. We suspect that the negative effect distance to highways have on property price is driven by .....

We now zoom into our **study area** to further understand highway effects in our region of interest.

### same interpretation but with 100m instead of 200m

For every 1% increase in distance from [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_i676 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, this means that if a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway, we can expect a similar property a block further from the highway to be about **`r paste0("$", round((2^coef_i676)*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** (assuming a block is about 100m). For every 1% increase in distance from [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_i76 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`, meaning a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway would be about **`r paste0("$", round((2^coef_i76)*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** if it were a block further from the highway. For every 1% increase in distance from [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_us1 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`, meaning a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway would be about **`r paste0("$", round((2^coef_us1)*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** if it were a block further from the highway.

The exception here is for properties within 500m of [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"}, where the beta coefficient for log distance to highway is `r coef_i95` (p < 0.001). For every 1% increase in distance from [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"}, property price decreases by `r paste0(round(abs(1.01^coef_i95 - 1), 4)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, this means that if a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway, we can expect a similar property a block further from the highway to be about **`r paste0("$", 100000 - round((2^coef_i95), 5)*100000)` less expensive**.

```{r prop500_res_scatter}
           color = closest_highway, fill = closest_highway)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .2, size = 0.3, show.legend = F) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", size = 1.2, show.legend = F) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("US-1" = "#1a9988",
                                "I-76" = "#eb5600",
                                "I-95" = "#eba075",
                                "I-676" = "#7fe3d6")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("US-1" = "#1a9988",
                               "I-76" = "#eb5600",
                               "I-95" = "#eba075",
                               "I-676" = "#7fe3d6")) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("US-1:", coef_res_us1),
                x = 4.25,
                y = 11.75),
            color = "#1a9988", 
            show.legend = F) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("I-76:", coef_res_i76),
                x = 4.25,
                y = 12.75),
            color = "#eb5600",
            show.legend = F) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("I-95:", coef_res_i95),
                x = 4.25,
                y = 13.25),
            color = "#eba075",
            show.legend = F) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("I-676:", coef_res_i676),
                x = 4.25,
                y = 13.75),
            color = "#7fe3d6",
            show.legend = F) +
  labs(title = "Residential Property Price (log) as a function of Distance to Closest Highway (log)",
       subtitle = "Properties within 500m of highways",
       x = "Log Distance to Closest Highway",
       y = "Log Property Price") +
  theme_minimal()

scatter_4highways_res

```

The scatter plot above shows the relationship between distance to highway and property price along with the regression coefficients for each highway. We observe that without controlling for anything else, property prices generally increase (albeit by very little) as we move away from a highway which tracks with our literature review of highway effects on property prices. 

When predicting property price, the beta coefficient for log distance to highway is `r coef_res_i676`, `r coef_res_i76`, and `r coef_res_us1` for [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, and [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, respectively (note that the though the beta coefficients were significant with p < 0.01 for [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"} and [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, it was not statistically significant for [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} with a p = 0.069). 

For every 1% increase in distance from [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_res_i676 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, this means that if a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway, we can expect a similar property a block further from the highway to be about **`r paste0("$", round((4^coef_res_i676)*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** (assuming a block is about 200m). For every 1% increase in distance from [I-76]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_res_i76 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`, meaning a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway would be about **`r paste0("$", round((4^coef_res_i76)*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** if it were a block further from the highway. For every 1% increase in distance from [US-1]{style="color: #1a9988;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^coef_res_us1 - 1, 4)*100,"%")`, meaning a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway would be about **`r paste0("$", round((4^coef_res_us1)*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** if it were a block further from the highway.

The exception here is for properties within 500m of [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"}, where the beta coefficient for log distance to highway is `r coef_res_i95` (p < 0.001). For every 1% increase in distance from [I-95]{style="color: #eba075;"}, property price decreases by `r paste0(round(abs(1.01^coef_res_i95 - 1), 4)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, this means that if a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway, we can expect a similar property a block further from the highway to be about **`r paste0("$", 100000 - round((4^coef_res_i95), 5)*100000)` less expensive**.

We now zoom into our **study area** to further understand highway effects in our region of interest.

### I-676 Effects

One of OTIS's key interests is the effect of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} on property prices nearby.  Here, we construct a relatively **simple linear model** with a few key predictors to look at the effect of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} on property prices while accounting for some control variables such as the square footage of the property, number of bathrooms, year built, zoning, and zip code among others.

For these analyses, we look at properties **within our study area**.

```{r i676effects_setup_studyareanew, quiet = TRUE, results = 'hide'}
# working with the newest philly_properties dataset where data was cleaned for our studyarea
property_studyarea_new <- st_read("Dataset/property_CT_FE.geojson") #1528 rows

# add features for simple linear regression
props_i676_tomodel <- property_studyarea_new %>% 
  # filter() %>% # there are a couple properties with total area < 100; reduces dataset to 990 properties
  # some feature engineering
  mutate(residential = ifelse(category_code_description %in% c("APARTMENTS  > 4 UNITS",
                                                               "MIXED USE",
                                                               "MULTI FAMILY",
                                                               "SINGLE FAMILY",
                                                               "GARAGE - RESIDENTIAL"),
                              1, 0), # is this property residential? (including mixed)
         
         building_code_description_new = case_when(
           grepl("FITNESS CENTER|GOV'T MUNICIPAL/STATE/FEDERAL", building_code_description_new) ~ "MostExpensive",
           grepl("LIFE CARE FACILITY-ASSTD LVNG|CORRECTIONAL|MEDICAL OFFICE BLDNG|PARKING GARAGE/DECK|BOARDING/ROOMING HOSUE|MIXED - RES/COMM|SCHOOL|BANK|OFFICE BLDNG - Mid Rise|DET MIXED-COM/RES-BLT AS COM", building_code_description_new) ~ "MoreExpensive",
           grepl("RETAIL - * SINGLE OCCUPANCY|ROW MIXED-COM/RES-BLT AS COM|ROW MODERN|APARTMENTS - LOW RISE|HOTEL - HI RISE|OFFICE BLDNG - Low Rise|FUNERAL HOME|RESTAURANT|DOWNTOWN ROW TYPE-* SNGL OCCP|WAREHOUSE|TWIN CONTEMPORARY|CAR WASH - AUTOMATIC|RETAIL CONDO|MANUFACTURING/PROCESSING|LOFT (INDUSTRIAL)|APARTMENTS - MID RISE|RELIGIOUS", building_code_description_new) ~ "Average",
           .default = "LeastExpensive" 
           ),
         building_code_description_new = factor(building_code_description_new),
      
         # all the other variables have been cleaned and feature engineered
) %>% 
  select(   # only keep vars necessary for model
    adj_sale_price,
    log_price, distance_to_I676, log_dist_highway,
    residential, 
    year_built, year_built_group,
    central_air, garage_spaces,
    number_of_bathrooms, number_of_bedrooms, total_area,
    exterior_condition, interior_condition, quality_grade,
    building_code_description_new, zoning_group,
    zip_code,
    I676_NS
  )

```

```{r RMSE_calculator}
getRMSE <- function(model_results) {
  # residual sum of squares
  rss <- c(crossprod(model_results$residuals))
  # Mean squared error:
  mse <- rss / length(model_results$residuals)
  # Root MSE:
  RMSE <- sqrt(mse)
  
  return(RMSE)
}

```

#### Model Results

```{r i676effects_model1_studyareanew}
# model with just distance to highway
model_i676 <- lm(log_price ~ log_dist_highway,
                 data = props_i676_tomodel)
# log_dist_highway  0.11110
# Multiple R-squared:  0.01228,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.01163

model_i676_summary <- summary(model_i676)
model_i676_RMSE <- getRMSE(model_i676)

# create a clean table to show model results
model_i676_table <- data.frame(model_i676_summary$coefficients) %>% 
  rename(p = `Pr...t..`) %>% 
  select(Estimate, p) %>% 
  mutate(Estimate = round(Estimate, 3),
         p = round(p, 3))
row.names(model_i676_table) <- c("Intercept", "Log Dist. to I-676")

model_i676_table %>% 
  kbl(align = c("l", rep("c", 2)),
      caption = "Regression Results: Log Price ~ Log Distance to I-676",
      col.names = c("Estimate", "p value")) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  kable_classic(full_width = F, html_font = "Cambria") %>% 
  row_spec(2, bold = T, background = "#7fe3d6") %>% 
  add_footnote(label = paste0("R-squared: ", round(model_i676_summary$r.squared, 3), ", RMSE: ", round(model_i676_RMSE, 3)),
               notation = "none")

```

From an overly simple model, just looking at how logged distance to [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} predicts logged property price, we see that for properties within 500m of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, distance from the highway does not have a large effect on property price. We see that for every 1% increase in distance to the highway, **property price increases by `r paste0(round(1.01^model_i676_table$Estimate[2] - 1, 4)*100,"%")`**. In more understandable terms, this means that if a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway, we can expect a similar property a block further from the highway to be about **`r paste0("$", round((4^model_i676_table$Estimate[2])*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** (assuming a block is about 200m). The R-squared value of the model is very low at `r round(model_i676_summary$r.squared, 3)` and the RMSE is very high `r round(model_i676_RMSE,3)`, meaning the model is terrible.

```{r i676effects_model2_studyareanew}
# simple model but with more predictors
model_i676_more <- lm(log_price ~ log_dist_highway + 
                        residential + building_code_description_new + zoning_group + # internal characteristics
                        year_built_group + central_air + 
                        number_of_bedrooms + number_of_bathrooms + total_area +
                        quality_grade + 
                        factor(zip_code), # neighborhood effects (via zip code for now)
                      data = props_i676_tomodel)

model_i676_more_summary <- summary(model_i676_more)
model_i676_more_RMSE <- getRMSE(model_i676_more)
# log_dist_highway                             0.101134640
# Multiple R-squared:  0.3585,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.3421

# create a clean table to show model results
model_i676_more_table <- data.frame(model_i676_more_summary$coefficients) %>% 
  rename(p = `Pr...t..`) %>% 
  select(Estimate, p) %>% 
  mutate(Estimate = round(Estimate, 3),
         p = round(p, 3))
row.names(model_i676_more_table) <- c("Intercept", "Log Dist. to I-676", "Residential", "Building Code - Least Exp.", "Building Code - More Exp.", "Building Code - Most Exp.", "Zoning - CMX3, 4", "Zoning - CMX5", "Zoning - ICMX", "Zoning - IRMX", "Zoning - Other", "Zoning - RM", "Zoning - RMX3", "Zoning - RSA5", "Year Built - New", "Year Built - Post-War Mid", "Year Built - Pre-War", "Year Built - Unknown", "Central Air - Unknown", "Central Air - Yes", "1 Bedrooms", "2 Bedrooms", "3 Bedrooms", "4 Bedrooms", "5 Bedrooms", "Unknown Num. Bedrooms", "1 Bathrooms", "2 Bathrooms", "3-5 Bathrooms", "6 Bathrooms", "7 Bathrooms", "Unknown Num. Bathrooms", "Total Area", "Quality Grade - Below Average", "Quality Grade - Good", "ZIP code - 19106", "ZIP code - 19107", "ZIP code - 19123", "ZIP code - 19130")

model_i676_more_table %>% 
  kbl(align = c("l", rep("c", 2)),
      caption = "Regression Results: Log Price ~ Log Distance to I-676 and Other Predictors",
      col.names = c("Estimate", "p value")) %>% 
  kable_styling() %>% 
  kable_classic(full_width = F, html_font = "Cambria") %>%
  row_spec(2, bold = T, background = "#7fe3d6") %>% 
  add_footnote(label = paste0("Adj. R-squared: ", round(model_i676_more_summary$adj.r.squared, 3), ", RMSE: ", round(model_i676_more_RMSE, 3)),
               notation = "none")

```

Finally, we look at a more robust model (which is still relatively simple, including only internal features of the property in addition to ZIP code and logged distance to [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}). This model includes the following predictors: year_built_group (categorical), quality_grade (categorical), number_of_bathrooms (categorical), number_of_bedrooms (categorical), total_area (continuous), central_air (categorical), building_code (categorical), zoning group (categorical), and a variable dictating whether the property is residential or not (binary). This more complex model does a better job at explaining the variance in property price than our previous two models, but is not optimal either. The **adjusted R-squared** for this model is **`r round(model_i676_more_summary$adj.r.squared, 3)`** and our **RMSE** is **`r round(model_i676_more_RMSE, 3)`**. 

When including these other predictors, the **effect of logged distance to [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} decreases** but remains statistically significant (beta coefficient of `r model_i676_more_table$Estimate[2]`). This means that for every 1% increase in distance from the highway, property price increases by `r paste0(round(abs(1.01^model_i676_more_table$Estimate[2] - 1), 4)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, this means that if a property that is \$100,000 is 50m away from the highway, we can expect a similar property a block further from the highway to be about **`r paste0("$", round((4^model_i676_more_table$Estimate[2])*100000) - 100000)` more expensive**.

### Discontinuity Effects

To complicate things even more, within our study area, we see that proximity to [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} has **different effects** on the [North (Callowhill)]{style="color: #eb5600;"} and [South (Chinatown)]{style="color: #1a9988;"} sides.

```{r discontinuity_data, quiet = TRUE, results = 'hide'}
# with most recently updated data (990 properties)
discontinuity_plot_ungrouped <- props_i676_tomodel %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(distance_to_I676m = distance_to_I676 * 0.3048,
         distance_to_highway = case_when(
           I676_NS == "north" ~ distance_to_I676m,
           I676_NS == "south" ~ -distance_to_I676m
           ))

discontinuity_plot <- discontinuity_plot_ungrouped%>% 
  group_by(distance_to_highway, I676_NS) %>%
  summarise(mean_log_price = mean(log_price, na.rm = T), .groups = "drop")

# median property prices on each side
med_north <- round(median(discontinuity_plot_ungrouped %>% 
                      filter(I676_NS == "north") %>% 
                      pull(adj_sale_price)))

med_south <- round(median(discontinuity_plot_ungrouped %>% 
                      filter(I676_NS == "south") %>% 
                      pull(adj_sale_price)))

# range of property prices on each side
range_north <- round(range(discontinuity_plot_ungrouped %>% 
                      filter(I676_NS == "north") %>% 
                      pull(adj_sale_price)))

range_south <- round(range(discontinuity_plot_ungrouped %>% 
                      filter(I676_NS == "south") %>% 
                      pull(adj_sale_price)))

```

```{r discontinuity_plot}
       x = "Distance to the Highyway (m)",

  # add annotations

                x = 250,

        plot.subtitle = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 12),

  labs(title = 'Logged Sale Price as a Function of Distance to I-676', 
       subtitle = glue("<span style='color:#1a9988;'>South Side</span> vs. <span style='color:#eb5600;'>North Side</span>"),
       x = "Distance to the Highyway (m)",
       y = "Log-transformed Sale Price") +
  
  # add annotations

             fill = "black", color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 5) +

                x = 250,
                y = 11.825),
            color = "#eb5600",
            show.legend = F) +
  geom_text(aes(label = coef_south,

```

In the plot above, we see that on the [North side]{style="color: #eb5600;"} of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, property prices remain relatively stable and unaffected by distance to the highway. The median property price in the [North]{style="color: #eb5600;"} is `r paste0("$", substr(med_north, 1, 3), ",", substr(med_north, 4, 6))`. When predicting logged property price, the beta coefficient for distance to highway is `r coef_north`, meaning the **highway has no effect on the price**.

On the other hand, in the [South side]{style="color: #1a9988;"} of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, property prices are within the same range of prices as in the [North side]{style="color: #eb5600;"}, but the median property price is slightly higher at `r paste0("$", substr(med_south, 1, 3), ",", substr(med_south, 4, 6))`. When predicting logged property price to the [South]{style="color: #1a9988;"} of the highway, the beta coefficient for distance to highway is `r coef_south`, meaning **distance to highway has a very small, positive effect on the price**. For every 1m increase in distance from [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}, property price increases by `r paste0(round(exp(coef_south)-1, 3)*100,"%")`. In more understandable terms, a property that is \$100,000 and 50m [South]{style="color: #1a9988;"} of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"} would be about **`r paste0("$", round((exp(coef_south)^150)*100000) - 100000)` more expensive** a block further from the highway.

This demonstrates that in our study area, the **highway has a very small influence on property price** that is only really seen on the [South side]{style="color: #1a9988;"} of [I-676]{style="color: #7fe3d6;"}.

## Modeling

Built on our simple OLS model, we train **four models** based on Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Regularized Linear Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost respectively for property price predictions:

+ **Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)** is a basic linear model that captures simple relationships but struggles with messy or complex data.

+ **Regularized Linear Regression (RLS)** improves on OLS by adding penalties to reduce overfitting, making it useful for datasets with many or irrelevant variables.

+ **Random Forest (RF)** averages many decision trees built on different data slices, handling complex patterns well but with less interpretability.

+ **XGBoost (XGB)** builds trees sequentially, each learning from the last’s errors, excelling in accuracy for structured data tasks.

After training and validation, the Random Forest model achieved the best performance among the tested models, with **a MAPE of 34.02% and a MAE of $214,118**, indicating a moderate level of accuracy, with average prediction errors of approximately one-third of actual prices. **The model performs particularly well for properties priced around $400,000 and demonstrates strong reliability for scenario-based forecasting in zoning categories such as RMX3, CMX3, and CMX4**. In contrast, its higher error rates in industrial zones and high-rise commercial areas (e.g., CMX5 and IRMX) reflect the more volatile and site-specific nature of property values in those markets, which may involve complex redevelopment potential or specialized land uses not fully captured by the model.

### Data Preparation

Based on feature engineering results, we select the xx most relevant features plus geographical location (longitude and latitude) as independent variables, and use log-transformed property price as the dependent variable. To build and evaluate our model, we split the dataset into two parts: **70%** as the training set to fit the model, and **30%** as the test set to evaluate its accuracy.

### Model Training

Within the training set, we use **spatial cross-validation**, which tests the model on different areas to avoid overfitting to nearby properties. **K-means Clustering** is used when creating the cross-validation folds. This helps prevent the model from "cheating" by seeing similar areas in both training and testing.

Each model is trained following a workflow, including defining, tuning, and evaluating. Here, we'd like to take **Random Forest workflow** as an example.

 1. `rf_plan` defines the Random Forest model structure. A Random Forest is a collection of many decision trees. Each tree looks at the data differently, and their combined result gives a more accurate and stable prediction.
 
 2. `rf_grid` is a grid of possible settings (combinations of `mtry` and `min_n`) used for tuning the random forest model. The `mtry` parameter controls how many predictors are randomly selected at each split in a tree, affecting model diversity and performance. The `min_n` parameter sets the minimum number of observations required to split a node, influencing tree depth and overfitting. By **evaluating different combinations of these hyperparameters**, the model can identify the configuration that yields the best predictive performance.
 
 3. `rf_wf` is a workflow that connects our preprocessing (`model_rec`) and model (`rf_plan`) together. It ensures that all the data is cleaned the same way every time we train or test the model.
 
 4. `rf_tuned` trains many Random Forest models using the different settings from `rf_grid`, and tests each one using our **spatial cross-validation folds**. This is the "try everything and see what works best" step. Each fold helps estimate how well the model will generalize.
 
 5. `rf_best_params` picks the best settings from the tuning process based on which combination gave the **lowest RMSE**. Then `rf_best_wf` finalizes the workflow with the best-performing parameters locked in.
 
 6. `rf_val_fit_geo` finally train the finalized Random Forest on the entire training set and test its accuracy on the test set. This gives the most realistic estimate of how well the model will perform on new, unseen property data.


```{r model_specifications, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Moedl Specifications
lm_plan <- 
  linear_reg() %>% 
  set_engine("lm")

glmnet_plan <- 
  linear_reg() %>% 
  set_args(penalty  = tune()) %>%
  set_args(mixture  = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet")

rf_plan <- rand_forest() %>%
  set_args(mtry  = tune()) %>%
  set_args(min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_args(trees = 1000) %>% # 3000 
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") %>% 
  set_mode("regression")

XGB_plan <- boost_tree() %>%
  set_args(mtry  = tune()) %>%
  set_args(min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_args(trees = 100) %>% # smaller
  set_engine("xgboost") %>% 
  set_mode("regression")

# Hyperparameter grid

glmnet_grid <- expand.grid(penalty = seq(0, 1, by = .25), 
                           mixture = seq(0,1,0.25))
rf_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2,5,10,13,30,45), 
                       min_n = c(50,100,150,200,250)) # 50-250
xgb_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2,5,10,13,30,45), 
                       min_n = c(50,100,150,200,250)) # same as rf

# create workflow
lm_wf <-
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(model_rec) %>% 
  add_model(lm_plan)
glmnet_wf <-
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(model_rec) %>% 
  add_model(glmnet_plan)
rf_wf <-
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(model_rec) %>% 
  add_model(rf_plan)
xgb_wf <-
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(model_rec) %>% 
  add_model(XGB_plan)

# Spatial CV approach
property_train_sf <- st_as_sf(property_train, coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326)
property_train_sf <- property_train_sf %>%
  mutate(
    Longitude = st_coordinates(.)[, 1],
    Latitude = st_coordinates(.)[, 2]
  )
set.seed(123)
cv_splits_zoning <- group_vfold_cv(property_train,
                                group = "zoning_group")
set.seed(123)
cv_splits_cluster <- spatial_clustering_cv(
  property_train_sf,
  v = 20,
  cluster_function = "kmeans"
)

cv_splits_geo <- cv_splits_cluster
control <- control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)
metrics <- metric_set(yardstick::rmse, yardstick::rsq, yardstick::mape, yardstick::smape)
```

```{r model_fit, eval=FALSE}
# fit model to workflow and calculate metrics
lm_tuned <- lm_wf %>%
  tune::fit_resamples(.,
                      resamples = cv_splits_geo,
                      control   = control,
                      metrics   = metrics)

glmnet_tuned <- glmnet_wf %>%
  tune::tune_grid(.,
                  resamples = cv_splits_geo,
                  grid      = glmnet_grid,
                  control   = control,
                  metrics   = metrics)

rf_tuned <- rf_wf %>%
  tune::tune_grid(.,
                  resamples = cv_splits_geo,
                  grid      = rf_grid,
                  control   = control,
                  metrics   = metrics)

xgb_tuned <- xgb_wf %>%
  tune::tune_grid(.,
                  resamples = cv_splits_geo,
                  grid      = xgb_grid,
                  control   = control,
                  metrics   = metrics)
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# 'Best' by some metric and margin

  last_fit(split     = data_split,
           control   = control,
           metrics   = metrics)

## Fit and Extract final model

# extract final fit model object as native package type
```

### Model Validation and Comparison

After applying the models to the test set, we evaluate and compare models' accuracy using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) and prediction v.s. actual value scatter plot.

+ **Mean Absolute Error (MAE)**: This tells us how much, on average, our model's predicted price is off from the real price. For example, if the model says a house is worth $310,000, but it actually sold for $300,000, the error is $10,000. MAE takes the average of all these errors. So if MAE is $15,000, that means our price predictions are usually off by about $15,000.

+ **Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)**: This tells us the size of the prediction error as a percentage of the real price. So instead of saying the model is off by $15,000, it might say it’s off by 5%. MAPE is useful when we're comparing predictions across properties with different price ranges.

+ **Prediction v.s. Actual Value Scatter Plot**: This is a chart that helps us see how close our model's predictions are to the actual sale prices. Each dot on the chart represents one property. If all the dots are near a straight diagonal line, it means the predictions are very close to the real prices. If they are scattered far away from that line, the model’s predictions are less accurate.

As a result, the **Random Forest model** shows the best performance, of which the price predictions are off by 34.02% ($214,118) on average.

```{r model_compare_data}
# Pull best hyperparam preds from out-of-fold predictions
lm_best_OOF_preds <- collect_predictions(lm_tuned) 

glmnet_best_OOF_preds <- collect_predictions(glmnet_tuned) %>% 
  filter(penalty  == glmnet_best_params$penalty[1] & mixture == glmnet_best_params$mixture[1])

rf_best_OOF_preds <- collect_predictions(rf_tuned) %>% 
  filter(mtry  == rf_best_params$mtry[1] & min_n == rf_best_params$min_n[1])

xgb_best_OOF_preds <- collect_predictions(xgb_tuned) %>% 
  filter(mtry  == xgb_best_params$mtry[1] & min_n == xgb_best_params$min_n[1])

# collect validation set predictions from last_fit model
lm_val_pred_geo     <- collect_predictions(lm_val_fit_geo)
glmnet_val_pred_geo <- collect_predictions(glmnet_val_fit_geo)
rf_val_pred_geo     <- collect_predictions(rf_val_fit_geo)
xgb_val_pred_geo    <- collect_predictions(xgb_val_fit_geo)


# Aggregate OOF predictions (they do not overlap with Validation prediction set)
OOF_preds <- rbind(data.frame(dplyr::select(lm_best_OOF_preds, .pred, log_adj_sale_price), model = "OLS"),
                   data.frame(dplyr::select(glmnet_best_OOF_preds, .pred, log_adj_sale_price), model = "RLS"),
                   data.frame(dplyr::select(rf_best_OOF_preds, .pred, log_adj_sale_price), model = "RF"),
                   data.frame(dplyr::select(xgb_best_OOF_preds, .pred, log_adj_sale_price), model = "XGB")) %>% 
  group_by(model) %>% 
  mutate(actual_price = exp(log_adj_sale_price) - 1,
         predicted_price = exp(.pred) - 1,
         RMSE = yardstick::rmse_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
         MAE  = yardstick::mae_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
         MAPE = mean(abs(predicted_price - actual_price) / actual_price)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels=c("OLS","RLS","RF","XGB")))

# Aggregate predictions from Validation set
# improve MAPE
val_preds <- rbind(data.frame(lm_val_pred_geo, model = "OLS"),
                   data.frame(glmnet_val_pred_geo, model = "RLS"),
                   data.frame(rf_val_pred_geo, model = "RF"),
                   data.frame(xgb_val_pred_geo, model = "XGB")) %>% 
  left_join(., property_modeling %>% 
              rowid_to_column(var = ".row") %>% 
              dplyr::select(Latitude, Longitude, zoning_group, .row), 
            by = ".row") %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  mutate(
    actual_price = exp(log_adj_sale_price) - 1,
    predicted_price = exp(.pred) - 1
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    RMSE = yardstick::rmse_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
    MAE  = yardstick::mae_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
    MAPE = mean(abs(predicted_price - actual_price) / actual_price)
  ) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(model = factor(model, levels=c("OLS","RLS","RF","XGB")))
```

Putting the validation results of train and test set altogether, **Random Forest model shows the best and a stable performance among the four models**. Though the Regularized Linear Regression (RLS) model behaves well with a MAPE of 50.92%, it predicts 10% more error than the RF model, indicating a low level of stability. Within the test set, **the price predictions of the RF model are off by 34.02% ($214,118) on average**, which is still a little high requiring further examination.

```{r model_compare_plot2}
  kable_styling() %>% 
  kable_classic(full_width = F, html_font = "Cambria") %>% 
  row_spec(3, bold = T, background = "#7fe3d6")
```

Predicted and observed prices are compared by the scatter plots. The [orange]{style="color: #eb5600;"} and [green]{style="color: #1a9988;"} lines are closer in the RF model, indicating a better performance overall. However, the deviation suggests that, **on average, the model’s predictions are lower than the observed prices**. Examining the data points further reveals that prediction accuracy decreases as prices rise, confirming our concerns about the variability in the higher price ranges of the dataset. The intersection point suggests that our **RF model performs better for lower-valued housing prices around $422,857.5**.

### Random Forest Model

Out of 1,529 properties in the study area, **460** were used for model validation. Beyond assessing overall prediction error statistics, we further evaluated the Random Forest model’s generalizability across different spatial contexts and zoning categories. The results indicate generally strong performance, with **prediction errors below 30% for residential and mixed-use properties**. In particular, the model proves to be reliable and generalizable for scenario-based forecasting focused on zoning types such as **RMX3, CMX3, and CMX4**.

```{r RF_data}
# join test data back to make spatial
val_pred_sf <- val_preds %>% 
  group_by(model) %>% 
  rowwise() %>% 
  mutate(RMSE = yardstick::rmse_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
    MAE  = yardstick::mae_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
    MAPE = mean(abs(predicted_price - actual_price) / actual_price)) %>% 
  st_as_sf(., coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"),
           remove = FALSE,
           crs = 4326)

val_pred_sf_plot <- val_pred_sf %>%
  filter(model == "RF")
Mean_MAPE <- mean(val_pred_sf_plot$MAPE)

# aggregate val error to zoning_group 
val_MAPE_by_zoning <- val_preds %>% 
  group_by(zoning_group, model) %>% 
  summarise(RMSE = yardstick::rmse_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
    MAE  = yardstick::mae_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
    MAPE = mean(abs(predicted_price - actual_price) / actual_price)) %>% 
  ungroup()

val_MAPE_by_zoning_plot <- val_MAPE_by_zoning %>%
  mutate(color = case_when(
    zoning_group %in% c("Other", "IRMX", "CMX5") ~ "#eb5600",
    !zoning_group %in% c("Other", "IRMX", "CMX5") ~ "#1a9988"
  ))
```

```{r RF_MAPE_plot}
ggplot(data = val_pred_sf_plot,aes(x = MAPE)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "#1a9988") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0,8,0.5)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of MAPE", 
       subtitle = "Random Forest model; Test set validation",
       # caption = "Figure 4.2",
       x = "Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept=mean(MAPE, na.rm=T)),
               color="#eb5600", linetype="dashed", size=1) +
  annotate(geom = "text", label = paste("Mean of MAPE:", paste0(round(Mean_MAPE*100, 2),"%")), # Insert correlation here
    x = .6, y = 120,
    hjust = 0, size = 4, color = "#eb5600")
```

```{r}
ggplot(val_pred_sf_plot %>% 
         filter(!MAPE<.34), 
       aes(x = log_adj_sale_price, y = .pred)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey", alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  geom_point(data = val_pred_sf_plot %>% 
               filter(MAPE<.34), 
             aes(x = log_adj_sale_price, y = .pred), 
             color = "#1a9988", alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "black", se = FALSE) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Observed value", y = "Predicted value",
       title = "Prediction Accuracy <span style='color:#1a9988;'>(Errors < 30%)</span>",
       subtitle = "Random Forest model; Test set validation") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_blank()
  )
```


With a mean MAPE of 34.02%, **most predictions deviate by less than 30%**, though some outliers are overestimated by as much as two to eight times the actual sale price. This indicates a moderate level of accuracy overall, with a long-tailed error distribution driven by a small number of extreme mispredictions.


```{r RF_MAPE_plot2}
# Create a continuous color palette for MAPE
pal_mape <- colorNumeric(
  palette = colorRampPalette(c("#7fe3d6","#eba075","#eb5600"))(50),
  domain = val_pred_sf_plot$MAPE
)

RF_MAPE_leaflet <- leaflet() %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addPolygons(data = studyarea_4326,
              color = "black",       # Black border
              weight = 4,            # Border thickness
              dashArray = "8,12",     # Dashed line pattern (5px on, 5px off)
              fill = FALSE) %>%
  # Points colored by MAPE
  addCircleMarkers(
    data = val_pred_sf_plot,
    color = ~pal_mape(MAPE),
    weight = 0.8,
    fillColor = ~pal_mape(MAPE),
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    radius = 3.5,
    popup = ~paste(
  "MAPE:", round(MAPE, 3), "<br>",
  "Zoning:", zoning_group, "<br>",
  "Property Price:", round(actual_price, 2), "<br>",
  "Predicted Price:", round(predicted_price, 2)
)) %>%
  
  # Add a legend for MAPE
  addLegend(
    pal = pal_mape,
    values = val_pred_sf_plot$MAPE,
    title = "MAPE",
    position = "bottomright"
  )

div(class = "center-leaflet", RF_MAPE_leaflet)
```

The distribution of prediction errors shows **no obvious spatial clustering**, suggesting that the model performs reasonably well in predicting future property prices across the study area.

```{r RF_MAPE_plot3}
# plot MAPE by zoning
ggplot(val_MAPE_by_zoning_plot, aes(x = reorder(zoning_group, MAPE), y = MAPE)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", aes(fill = color), width = .7, alpha = .7) +
  scale_fill_identity() + 
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0,6,0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Re-categorized zoning type",
       title = "MAPE by Zoning Group",
       subtitle = "Random Forest model; Test set validation") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = -45, hjust = 0)
  )
```

In the previous OLS model (Section 3.3.3.1), property price showed a strong relationship with zoning type, suggesting that **zoning serves as a meaningful proxy for how property value is perceived and regulated in practice**. For example, properties located in higher-density commercial zones such as CMX-4 or CMX-5 tended to exhibit significantly higher prices compared to those in residential zones like RM-1 or RSA-5. This reflects the **greater development potential and permitted uses in commercial mixed-use zones**, which typically allow for larger floor-area ratios (FAR), more flexible building types, and access to high-traffic areas—factors that increase market demand and drive up land value.

This pattern may also explain a preference for using the model’s predictions in future planning scenarios. Our random forest model shows high error rates in zones such as Unknown, SPPOA, CMX5, and IRMX, with some predictions exceeding four times the actual price. However, **it performs relatively well in RMX3, CMX3, and CMX4**, zones that are primarily residential or commercial mixed-use and are central to future zoning changes and community impact. While the model has an overall MAPE of 34%, its stronger performance in RMX and CMX zones suggests it is more reliable and generalizable for **scenario-based forecasting** focused on these zoning types.


```{r RF_without_zoning_plot}
# Filtered results
RF_filtered_results <- val_pred_sf_plot %>% 
  filter(!zoning_group %in% c("IRMX", "CMX5", "Other")) %>% 
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(
    RMSE = yardstick::rmse_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
    MAE  = yardstick::mae_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
    MAPE = paste0(round(100 * mean(abs(predicted_price - actual_price) / actual_price), 2), "%"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(zoning_scope = "Without IRMX, CMX5, Other")

# Unfiltered results
RF_all_results <- val_pred_sf_plot %>% 
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(
    RMSE = yardstick::rmse_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
    MAE  = yardstick::mae_vec(actual_price, predicted_price),
    MAPE = paste0(round(100 * mean(abs(predicted_price - actual_price) / actual_price), 2), "%"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(zoning_scope = "All Zoning")

# Combine
RF_combined_results <- bind_rows(RF_all_results, RF_filtered_results) %>%
  relocate(zoning_scope, .after = model)

# Display table
RF_combined_results %>%
  kbl(align = c("c", "c", "c", "c"),
      caption = "Validation Results by Zoning Scope") %>%
  kable_styling() %>%
  kable_classic(full_width = FALSE, html_font = "Cambria") %>% 
  row_spec(2, bold = T, background = "#7fe3d6")
```

Excluding industrial zones and high-rise office buildings from the analysis (IRMX, CMX5), the validation results show a MAPE of 30.21% and a MAE of $198,983.6, representing **an improvement of approximately 4% points in error and a reduction of over $20,000 in average absolute deviation compared to the full-sample predictions**. This suggests that the model performs more accurately when focused on residential and mixed-use properties, which are more consistent in pricing patterns and better represented in the training data. In contrast, **industrial parcels and high-density commercial zones** like CMX5 often exhibit highly variable and site-specific values driven by factors such as floor-area bonuses, special-use permits, and redevelopment potential—factors that are **difficult to capture with general property features alone**.
